Takeaway. SemNav improves evidence quality mainly by reduc-
ing irrelevant context, not by reducing coverage.
Downstream Repair Utility
To test whether the localization gains transfer to issue res-
olution, we use the context produced by each Gemma 4B
localizer as the only repository context available to two fixed
repair models, Gemma 4B and Qwen3.5 35B-A3B. We hold
the repair prompt, generation budget, patch validation, and
SWE-bench Lite test harness fixed across localization meth-
ods. Each model makes one deterministic repair attempt.
Applied measures whether a generated patch can be applied
to the repository, while Resolved requires it to pass the bench-
mark evaluation.
SemNav provides the best non-oracle context for both re-
pair models (Table 3). It improves the resolved rate over
the strongest baseline by 4.33 points with Gemma 4B and by
8.33 points with Qwen3.5 35B-A3B, while also achieving the
highest patch application rate. The benefit with both models
shows that SemNav’s localization gains transfer across repair
backends. The larger gain with Qwen suggests that a stronger
repair model can make effective use of the localized context.
SemNav remains below oracle context with both repair
models, showing that better localization can further improve
downstream repair. However, oracle context does not resolve
every issue, so patch generation remains a separate source of
error.
Takeaway. SemNav’s localization gains translate into better repair
performance across both backends.
Related Work
Repository-Level Issue Localization
Repository-level issue localization follows either predefined
workflows or agent-directed search. Workflow methods re-
trieve, filter, and rerank locations: Agentless localizes hier-
archically from repository structure to fine-grained entities,
SWE-Fixer combines lexical retrieval with learned local-
ization, SweRank applies task-specific retrieval and listwise
reranking, and CoSIL searches module- and function-level
call graphs in stages (Xia et al. 2025; Xie et al. 2025; Reddy
et al. 2026; Jiang et al. 2025). Agent-driven methods let an
LLM acquire evidence through AST search, repository-graph
traversal, action scheduling, language-server navigation, or
shell tools (Zhang et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2025; Yu et al. 2025;
Zhang et al. 2026b; Sutawika et al. 2026). Some systems re-
tain candidate locations or repository knowledge outside the
reasoning trajectory (Jiang et al. 2025; Yu et al. 2025; Ma
et al. 2025a). SemNav combines broad deterministic initial-
ization with evidence-backed agent revision.
Repository Representation and Navigation
Repository representations range from cross-file code frag-
ments (Zhang et al. 2023; Ding et al. 2024; Liang et al. 2024)
to graphs of files, classes, functions, and syntax-derived
relations. RepoGraph retrieves local definition and refer-
ence neighborhoods, CodexGraph supports structured graph
queries, LocAgent traverses a heterogeneous entity graph,
and CoSIL uses stage-specific call graphs (Ouyang et al.
2025; Liu et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2025; Jiang et al. 2025).
RepoNavigator further provides language-server-backed def-
inition navigation (Zhang et al. 2026b), while complemen-
tary methods attach natural-language descriptions or con-
ceptual concerns to entities for semantic retrieval (Athale
and Vaddina 2025; Wang et al. 2025). Yet syntax-derived
relations may leave targets ambiguous, and structural, se-
mantic, and source evidence often remain separate. Sem-
Nav unifies on-demand language-server-resolved relations
and issue-conditioned Semantic Cards around shared graph

entities, enabling reuse of both evidence types throughout
localization.
Conclusion
We propose SemNav, a framework for repository-level is-
sue localization that combines broad deterministic retrieval
with agent-driven investigation. Through a Semantic Navi-
gation Graph, Semantic Cards, and a Candidate Workspace,
SemNav makes repository relations, entity interpretations,
and evidence-grounded candidate judgments explicit and re-
visable throughout localization. Experiments across bench-
marks and models demonstrate improved localization accu-
racy and evidence quality, reduced context requirements for
the Localization Agent, and better downstream issue resolu-
tion.

title: Improving Visual Sensitivity of LLMs on Multimodal Machine Translation with Metric-based Loss Weighting
abstract: Multimodal Machine Translation aims to incorporate additional signal from non-textual modalities to improve translations by resolving ambiguities. While models, through multimodal fusion, are able to accept images related to the source text, they can ignore this information. Therefore, increasing their visual sensitivity remains an active research area. In this work, we introduce a training method, Metric-based Loss Weighting, that improves visual grounding of translations by increasing the loss function for tokens that benefit from the accompanying image. We identify these tokens using the Point-wise Cross-mutual Information (PCXMI) metric, which compares the model's output probabilities with and without visual context. We introduce a Congruency-based PCXMI metric and experimentally show that both metrics working in combination yield the best results. We evaluate our method by fine-tuning three pretrained Multimodal Large Language Models on the task of Image-guided Machine Translation for three language directions. Metric-based Loss Weighting outperforms other tested methods on the CoMMuTE contrastive dataset, improving accuracy by up to more than 7 percentage points compared to standard fine-tuning, while maintaining strong general translation performance.
content:
Improving Visual Sensitivity of LLMs on Multimodal Machine Translation
with Metric-based Loss Weighting
Paweł M ˛aka1, Piotr Andruszkiewicz2, 3, Yusuf Can Semerci1, Jan Scholtes1,
Gerasimos Spanakis1
1Department of Advanced Computing Sciences, Maastricht University
2Warsaw University of Technology
3IDEAS Research Institute
{pawel.maka, y.semerci, j.scholtes, jerry.spanakis}@maastrichtuniversity.nl
piotr.andruszkiewicz@pw.edu.pl
Abstract
Multimodal Machine Translation aims to in-
corporate additional signal from non-textual
modalities to improve translations by resolv-
ing ambiguities. While models, through mul-
timodal fusion, are able to accept images re-
lated to the source text, they can ignore this
information.
Therefore, increasing their vi-
sual sensitivity remains an active research area.
In this work, we introduce a training method,
Metric-based Loss Weighting, that improves
visual grounding of translations by increasing
the loss function for tokens that benefit from
the accompanying image. We identify these
tokens using the Point-wise Cross-mutual In-
formation (PCXMI) metric, which compares
the model’s output probabilities with and with-
out visual context. We introduce a Congruency-
based PCXMI metric and experimentally show
that both metrics working in combination yield
the best results. We evaluate our method by
fine-tuning three pretrained Multimodal Large
Language Models on the task of Image-guided
Machine Translation for three language direc-
tions. Metric-based Loss Weighting outper-
forms other tested methods on the CoMMuTE
contrastive dataset, improving accuracy by up
to more than 7 percentage points compared to
standard fine-tuning, while maintaining strong
general translation performance.
1
Introduction
Sentence-level Machine Translation (MT) systems
achieved high performance (Vaswani et al., 2017;
Hassan et al., 2018; Costa-jussà et al., 2022; Tiede-
mann et al., 2024), but they are inherently lim-
ited by the lack of context. In Multimodal Ma-
chine Translation (MMT), the additional signal
from other modalities can improve translation in
cases where text alone is ambiguous. This signal
can be audio, video, or image (Sulubacak et al.,
2020; Garg et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2025). In this
study, we concentrate our efforts on Image-based
MT.
While the images are available to the MMT sys-
tems, the reliance on the other modality is not
guaranteed. Indeed, Elliott (2018) did not find
the expected performance drop of the tested sys-
tems after randomly replacing images. Wu et al.
(2021) attributed some gains of the MMT systems
to regularization. Therefore, visual sensitivity of
the MMT models has seen increased attention from
researchers in recent years (Sato et al., 2023; Zhu
et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2024; Bowen et al., 2024;
Futeral et al., 2025).
As traditional translation metrics such as
BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) are not sensitive
enough to judge disambiguations, we turn towards
CoMMuTE (Futeral et al., 2023). It is a contrastive
dataset where the tested models are presented with
multiple possible translations of the ambiguous
source sentence and tasked with selecting the cor-
rect one. The selection is based on the probability
that models give to each option, and the final metric
is the accuracy of assigning the highest probability
to the correct one.
The field of MMT went from training special-
ized architectures from random initialization (Yin
et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021) to using pre-trained
models as building blocks and fine-tuning the re-
sulting model with multimodal parallel data (Gupta
et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2025). Recently, more fo-
cus has been given to Multimodal Large Language
Models (MLLMs) (Alayrac et al., 2022; Liu et al.,
2023; Laurençon et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025) due
to their generalizability and strong performance in
different tasks (Zhu et al., 2024). In this study, we
concentrate on methods that could be used to en-
hance fine-tuning of MLLMs on the task of MMT
to increase the visual grounding of the translation.
We argue that the insufficient number of exam-
1
arXiv:2609.31169v1  [cs.CL]  25 Sep 2026

Figure 1: The illustration of Metric-based Loss Weighting: (1) Calculate the image dependence metric for each
token (PCXMI), based on the model’s output probabilities with and without an image (or with an incongruent
image); (2) Fine-tune the model with increased loss (by α) for the identified tokens (with PCXMI larger than τ).
ples in the widely used MMT training datasets
that require images for correct translation is caus-
ing the training signal to be sparse and, therefore,
not enough for the models to learn to rely on con-
text (Futeral et al., 2023). To mitigate this issue,
we propose a training strategy where we identify
the tokens in the target sequence that benefit from
context and, subsequently, increase the loss for
those tokens during training. To identify the image-
dependent tokens, we use the Point-wise Cross-
Mutual Information (PCXMI) metric (Fernandes
et al., 2023), which compares the output proba-
bilities of the model in two situations: with and
without the context (see Figure 1). We propose a
modification to this metric by using an incongruent
image as context instead of the lack of it. We com-
bine both metrics to achieve the best results. We
test our method against several techniques adapted
to fine-tuning of MLLMs using three models and
three language directions. Our Metric-based Loss
Weighting method outperforms the baselines in
terms of CoMMuTE accuracy on most of the tested
scenarios. It improves the accuracy by up to more
than 7 percentage points compared to the standard
fine-tuning.
Our contributions are as follows:
1. We introduce a training strategy for fine-tuning
MLLMs that improves their visual sensitivity on
the task of MMT based on identifying and increas-
ing loss function for image-dependent tokens.
2. We adapt the Point-wise Cross-Mutual Informa-
tion (PCXMI) metric (Fernandes et al., 2023) to
MMT, introduce Congruency-based PCXMI met-
ric, and experimentally show that both metrics
working in combination yield best results.
3. We adapt and evaluate several existing meth-
ods for fine-tuning MLLMs on the task of MMT,
establishing the baseline for future research.
4. We show that the pre-trained models exhibit
high visual sensitivity which can be further in-
creased with specialized fine-tuning techniques.
5. We empirically confirm the discrepancy be-
tween traditional translation metrics such as
BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and the image re-
liance of the MLLMs.
2
Related Work
Researchers have been interested in incorporating
the information coming from other modalities to
enhance text-to-text translation (Sulubacak et al.,
2020; Garg et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2025). While
this includes audio and video (Gu et al., 2021; Li
et al., 2023), large focus has been concentrated
on single images related to the source text (Elliott
et al., 2017; Barrault et al., 2018; Cheng et al.,
2024; Futeral et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). The
methods proposed specialized architectures concen-
trating on feature extraction (Yao and Wan, 2020;
Fang and Feng, 2022), cross-modal fusion and
alignment (Zhao et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2022),
and cross-modal attention (Nishihara et al., 2020;
Gupta et al., 2023).
Other notable directions include: employing aux-
iliary tasks, such as Visually Conditioned Masked
Language Modeling (VMLM) (Futeral et al., 2023,
2025), image captioning (Gupta et al., 2023), or
visual question answering (Zhang et al., 2025; Gao
et al., 2025), masking the source sentence to in-
crease visual grounding (Sato et al., 2023; Cheng
2

et al., 2024; Bowen et al., 2024), and data aug-
mentation by image generation (Long et al., 2021;
Li et al., 2022c; Chen et al., 2025), using text-to-
image models (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Rombach
et al., 2022), or backtranslation (Li et al., 2021).
The MMT models are often trained on the widely
used Multi30k dataset and evaluated on the accom-
panying testsets (Elliott et al., 2016, 2017; Barrault
et al., 2018). Although the systems show increased
BLEU scores (Papineni et al., 2002) compared to
the text-only baselines, the benefits have been at-
tributed to regularization (Wu et al., 2021). For
example, Elliott (2018), after replacing the relevant
images with random ones, did not see the expected
drop in performance. This could be caused by the
insufficient number of examples in the Multi30k
training dataset that require context in the form
of the accompanying image for correct transla-
tion (Futeral et al., 2023).
Earlier works trained models from random ini-
tialization (Yin et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021), but in-
creasingly often researchers utilize pretrained mod-
els (Gupta et al., 2023; Futeral et al., 2025; Yu et al.,
2025). This transition is motivated by the strong
generalization capabilities of the pretrained models,
acquired through training on large amounts of data.
The popular models include CLIP (Radford et al.,
2021) and BLIP (Li et al., 2022b) for image feature
extraction, and Large Language Models, such as
mBART (Liu et al., 2020) or Qwen (Yang et al.,
2025), for text understanding and generation.
The emergence of strong general-purpose Multi-
modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), capable
of incorporating visual information without archi-
tectural modifications, presents a potential shift
in the approach to Multimodal Machine Transla-
tion (Alayrac et al., 2022; Awadalla et al., 2023; Bai
et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024). While Xiong and
Zhao (2025) and Yu et al. (2025) evaluated their
methods against MLLMs, and Zhu et al. (2024)
performed a large scale evaluation of publicly-
available MLLMs, we concentrate on instruction-
tuning (Wei et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026; Hu
et al., 2022) and evaluating the open-weights mod-
els (Laurençon et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025).
Our method is inspired by Metric-based Fine-
tuning and Loss Weighting, the two separate tech-
niques introduced for encoder-decoder models by
M ˛aka et al. (2025) for the task of Context-aware
MT. Importantly, both techniques used only a tex-
tual modality, and the loss weighting was based on
the external annotations. In this work, we combine
both techniques, and adapt it to the multimodal
setting of Image-guided MT. Furthermore, we in-
troduce a new Metric that uses incongruent images
instead of not providing an image.
3
Method
Our proposed method consists of two steps. First,
we identify which tokens in the target sentence re-
quire context. To do this, we measure how much
the output probabilities of the pretrained model
change when the context image is present or not
(alternatively, when the image is not related to the
text). Second, we use this information during train-
ing to improve the visual sensitivity of the model
by increasing the loss corresponding to the context-
dependent tokens.
Similar to M ˛aka et al. (2025), we employ the
Point-wise Cross-Mutual Information (PCXMI)
metric Fernandes et al. (2023) for the identifica-
tion step. The original PCXMI metric compares
the model’s output probabilities with and without
previous sentences as context. We adapt it to the
setting of Image-guided MT by treating the accom-
panying image as context. The equation below
calculates the PCXMI for the j-th token in the
target sequence:
PCXMIj = logq (yj|yt<j, x, C)

x. Crucially, the model has to be able to perform

Additionally, we propose a modification to the

We refer to this metric as

In practice, both metrics rely on the outputs of

towards the tokens for which it already exhibits

4
Experiments
We experimentally evaluated the effects of our
method on fine-tuning MLLMs on the task of MMT.
We are specifically interested in observing how it
affects the visual sensitivity of the tested models.
We experimented with three popular open-
weights
instruction-tuned
models:
Qwen3-
VL 4B Instruct1, Qwen3-VL 8B Instruct2 (Bai
et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025), and IDEFICS
9B Instruct3 (Laurençon et al., 2023). We used
LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) to fine-tune the models
on the Multi30k dataset (Elliott et al., 2016). We
experimented with three language directions:
English-to-German,
English-to-French,
and
English-to-Czech.
We compared our method with the following
baselines:
• Fine-tuning - simply fine-tuning the model on
the Image-guided MT training dataset.
• Visually Conditioned Masked Language
Modeling (VMLM) - fine-tuning with the aux-
iliary task, where the model is presented with the
source sentence containing masked tokens, and it
has to predict those masked tokens (Futeral et al.,
2023, 2025). We mask words with the probability p,
which is a hyper-parameter, with a string MASK{n},
where n goes from 1 to the total number of masked
words in the source text. Because VMLM does
not require a parallel corpus, often an additional
multimodal dataset in the source language is used.
In our setting, we use only the Multi30k dataset,
discarding the target-side sentences, to keep the
methods using comparable amounts of data.
• Metric-based Fine-tuning - we adapt this
method from the original text-only version (M ˛aka
et al., 2025). After the initial fine-tuning, we cal-
culate the PCXMI and CPCXMI metrics and se-
lect top-k examples with the highest maximum
values of the calculated metrics for further fine-
tuning. We take the maximum of the two metrics,
as this yielded better results in the preliminary ex-
periments than either of the metrics on their own.
• Word Dropout - dropping random tokens
from the source sentence to force the model to
use the image to improve translation, adapted to
Image-guided Machine Translation from CoWord
Dropout (Fernandes et al., 2021). The probability
of dropping out a token is controlled by the hyper-
parameter p. In the preliminary experiments, we
determined that dropout on the word-level was bet-
ter than token-level. Therefore, we drop out words
based on the Moses Tokenizer4(Koehn et al., 2007).

sensitivity of the fine-tuned models, we employ
the CoMMuTE contrastive dataset (Futeral et al.,
2023). In this dataset, the models are presented
with an image, an ambiguous source sentence, and
two possible translations, where the correct one
depends on the accompanying image. The dataset
measures the accuracy of the models by assign-
ing higher probabilities to correct target sentences.
Following Futeral et al. (2023), we repeated the
experiments three times with different seeds and
averaged the results.

In terms of BLEU and COMET, Qwen3-VL 8B
exhibited better performance than the other two
models, with IDEFICX 9B scoring lower than the
smaller Qwen-VL 4B model on all language di-
rections. While this could be caused by different
generation method (no sampling for the IDEFICX
model), this gap is removed after fine-tuning on
the Multi30k dataset. The CoMMuTE accuracy of
the baseline models is similar between English-to-
German and English-to-French, and there is a clear
drop for English-to-Czech for Qwen-3-VL 4B and
IDEFICS 9B models (more than 6 and 4 percent-
age points, respectively). This could be attributed
to lower amounts of English-to-Czech parallel and
Czech monolingual data in the training corpora.
For English-to-German, fine-tuning reduces the
visual grounding, as measured by the CoMMuTE
accuracy, compared to the baseline model. Only
Word Dropout and Metric-based Loss Weighting re-
trieve and surpass the performance of the baseline
model. This effect is not visible for the two re-
maining language directions, where each technique
improves the baseline performance. We hypoth-
esize that the drop in CoMMuTE accuracy from
English to German stems from linguistic proxim-
ity (both are Germanic languages). This proximity
may make the translation task easier for the models
to learn during fine-tuning, reducing their reliance
on the visual modality to resolve ambiguity. We
leave evaluating this hypothesis for future work.
VMLM did not yield large improvements in visual
sensitivity compared to other methods. We attribute
this to our use of only a parallel multimodal dataset
for this task. We expect it to show larger improve-
ments when trained on a large-scale monolingual
multimodal dataset. However, training it already
used twice as much computational resources com-
pared to other methods (see Appendix A), and scal-
6

ing it further falls outside the scope of this work.
While the highest results of CoMMuTE accu-
racy are significantly different from the baseline
models and Fine-tuning (according to Welch’s t-
test), due to the low number of runs, the results
for the top methods (marked as bold and under-
lined in the result tables) are not significantly dif-
ferent. Nevertheless, Metric-based Loss Weight-
ing achieved the highest results in terms of CoM-
MuTE accuracy on 6 out of 9 experimental set-
tings, and achieved the second-best result for the
remaining three. Word Dropout showed the best
result in three settings and was the second best
in four of them.
Source Degradation achieved
the second best result on English-to-French with
the Qwen3-VL 4B model, and Metric-based Fine-
tuning on English-to-Czech with the same model.
Notably, the high score on CoMMuTE does not cor-
relate well with the achieved BLEU and COMET
scores, indicating that the general translation qual-
ity and visual grounding are not necessarily mutual,
which corroborates the findings of Futeral et al.
(2025). This can be attributed to the examples
in the Multi30k testsets not requiring images for
good translation (Caglayan et al., 2019; Wu et al.,
2021). We further investigate this phenomenon
in Section 5.2, where we qualitatively analyze the
selected translations in the MSCOCO English-to-
French dataset.
5
Analysis
In this section, we take a deeper look at the PCXMI
and CPCXMI distributions. Next, we examine
translation examples produced by our method and
standard fine-tuning. Lastly, we experiment with
combining our method with Word Dropout, another
technique that achieves strong results. Additionally,
in Appendix B we present the ablation study.
5.1
Metrics Analysis
In Figure 2, we present two examples of the per-
token values of the PCXMI and CPCXMI met-
rics. Further examples can be found in Appendix C.
While both metrics are capable of identifying the
tokens that require image for disambiguation, they
are not perfect, and can ignore or misidentify those
tokens. This can be partially mitigated by taking
the maximum of both metrics.
In Appendix C, we present the distributions of
the calculated metrics (PCXMI, CPCXMI, and
their maximum) on the training subset of the
Multi30k dataset for each tested model and lan-
guage direction. The values of the metrics depend
heavily on the model, as can be seen in the dif-
ference between both the Qwen3-VL models and
IDEFICS 9B. The difference between language
directions for the same model is a lot smaller. Ad-
ditionally, all distributions show a concentration of
values close to zero and a long tail at high values.
This means that most examples in the dataset do not
require, according to the tested models, images to
disambiguate. The distributions for Multi30k and
CoMMute datasets are compared in Appendix C,
where we show that the distribution for the latter is
denser for higher values of the metric.
5.2
Qualitative Analysis
In this section, we investigate the drop in BLEU
exhibited by Metric-based Loss Weighting com-
pared to Fine-tuning seen for Qwen3-VL 8B on the
English-to-French language direction. We perform
the qualitative analysis of the translations of the
MSCOCO testset, where the difference in BLEU
between the methods is the largest. In Figure 3,
we present the distributions of per-example BLEU
scores for Fine-tuning and our method. They differ
mostly in two regions: (1) BLEU scores around
100, where Fine-tuning has more examples, (2)
BLEU scores around 30, where the Weighting dis-
tribution is denser.
We examined the examples that exhibit the high-
est difference in BLEU between Fine-tuning and
our method (both ways, with both Fine-tuning and
our method achieving better scores). We found
that the largest drop in example-level BLEU scores
mostly corresponds to acceptable translations that
differ from the gold target translation. More exam-
ples with our descriptions and further details of the
analysis are presented in Appendix D.
5.3
Combining Weighting with Dropout
The main results of the tested methods show that
Metric-based Loss Weighting achieves the highest
CoMMuTE accuracy. The second best perform-
ing method, Word Dropout, modifies the source
side and is technically not related to our method,
which changes the training signal corresponding
to the target side. In this section, we test whether
the combination of both methods could increase
the visual sensitivity of the resulting models even
further.
For each example, the Metric-based Loss
Weighting is applied (as described in Section 3).

6
Conclusions
This work introduced a training strategy for fine-
tuning MLLMs for the task of MMT that increases
the visual grounding during translation.
It in-
creases the loss for the tokens that benefit from
context in the form of the image, as measured by
the Point-wise Cross-Mutual Information (PCXMI)
and Congruency-based PCXMI (CPCXMI). Both
metrics rely on the model’s output probabilities
with and without the image (or with incongruent
image in case of CPCXMI).
We empirically tested our technique against ex-
isting methods adapted for the task of fine-tuning
MLLMs on three models and three language di-
rections, and showed its increased performance
8

in terms of CoMMuTE accuracy, while maintain-
ing strong overall translation quality, as measured
by BLEU and COMET. Our results confirm that
general-purpose translation metrics (BLEU and
COMET) fail to capture how strongly models rely
on visual modality for MMT. In future work, we
will explore how the metrics can inform masking
and word dropout on the source side.
7
Limitations
While we investigate three language directions and
three sub-families, all of them come from the Indo-
European family, and all use the Latin script. This
limitation was imposed by the language directions
covered by both Multi30k and CoMMuTE datasets.
We suspect that the measured performance of the
methods goes beyond the tested language pairs, but
this claim has not been tested experimentally. Due
to the low number of repeated runs and the vari-
ability of the measured metrics, the results of the
top methods are not different with statistical sig-
nificance. We limited our investigation to only the
same multimodal parallel dataset for each method,
while VMLM could use additional multimodal
monolingual data.
For Metric-based Loss Weighting, we calculate
the image dependence metrics using the baseline
models. Updating the metrics during training or
using a separate (presumably more visually sen-
sitive) model could yield different results, but we
did not test this setting. Furthermore, we limit our
method to PCXMI and CPCXMI, and a broader ex-
ploration of image dependence metrics could lead
to increased performance. Finally, while we tested
the methods on three MLLMs, their sizes were
limited to less than 10B parameters.

Training Details
We trained the models using the AdamW opti-
mizer (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019). We used
a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 24GB for
Qwen3-VL 4B, and a single NVIDIA A100 40GB
for Qwen3-VL 8B and IDEFICS 9B. The average
training times per epoch for each model are pre-
sented in Table 5. The time for Metric-based Fine-
tuning is shown only for the second stage training
(training on the top-k examples). The training time
for VMLM is roughly doubled compared to fine-
tuning, because of the auxiliary task of masked
12

language modeling.
The times for other meth-
ods are comparable, meaning that additional pre-
processing (dropout, masking) and post-processing
(loss weighting) do not meaningfully increase the
training time compared to basic fine-tuning. The
training was performed on the Multi30k dataset
and evaluated on its testsets and the CoMMuTE
contrastive dataset. The sizes of the used datasets
can be found in Table 6.

• Visually Conditioned Masked Language

• Metric-based Fine-tuning - learning rate val-

D
Extended Qualitative Analysis
To examine the source of the largest measured drop
in BLEU between Fine-tuning and Metric-based
Loss Weighting in our experiments, we analyzed
the translations of Qwen3-VL 8B on MSCOCO
English-to-French testset of the runs with seed 1,
which also shows the highest BLEU difference. We
looked at the 20 examples with the highest differ-
ence of example-level BLEU scores between the
two methods (20 in each direction). The selected in-
stances for Fine-tuning scoring higher can be seen
in Figure 8, and in Figure 9 for Weighting scor-
ing higher. We categorize the causes of the drop
in BLEU into three categories: (1) change of the
tense (mostly present continuous instead of present
simple), (2) synonyms or equivalent expressions,
(3) true errors including omissions and incorrect

meaning. Out of the 20 instances with highest drop
of BLEU for Weighting 30% were due to the use
of a different form, 45% were equivalent, and 25%
were erroneous. From the 20 instances where Fine-
tuning showed the largest drop in BLEU 10% were
due to a different form, 50% were synonyms, and
40% contained errors. While this analysis only
looked at the selected examples, it shows that the
largest drop in example-level BLEU scores mostly
corresponds to acceptable translations that differ
from the gold target translation.

title: Neural State Prediction: Obstructing Shortcut Learning in EEG Foundation Models
abstract: EEG foundation models increasingly use masked prediction to learn from unlabeled recordings, but optimizing this objective does not ensure transferable neural representations. A central challenge is that stable positional cues and local correlations can make masked regions predictable without integrating distributed neural context. To reduce this reliance on low-information prediction paths, we introduce Neural State Prediction (NSP), a latent-predictive framework that constrains both the prediction target and the available context. NSP uses a Target Encoder updated by an exponential moving average (EMA) to define latent supervision. Identity residualization removes additive effects associated with channel identity and relative time from the targets, while topology-separated context excludes their immediate spatial and temporal neighborhood from the visible input. We pretrain NSP on 2.2 million EEG segments from TUEG and evaluate it across 30 downstream datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, emotion recognition, motor imagery, event-related potentials, cognitive-state decoding, and language retrieval. Under full-parameter multi-task fine-tuning on EEG-FM-Bench, NSP achieves 63.94 macro balanced accuracy across 14 datasets, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.35 percentage points. Controlled component ablations assess the contribution of each mechanism, while matched context controls and held-out interventions characterize the role of context geometry, signal content, and positional information. Jointly designing latent targets and their context offers a promising direction for EEG foundation models that learn from distributed signal structure.

ABSTRACT
EEG foundation models increasingly use masked prediction to learn from unla-
beled recordings, but optimizing this objective does not ensure transferable neu-

correlations can make masked regions predictable without integrating distributed
neural context. To reduce this reliance on low-information prediction paths, we
introduce Neural State Prediction (NSP), a latent-predictive framework that con-
strains both the prediction target and the available context. NSP uses a Target
Encoder updated by an exponential moving average (EMA) to define latent super-
vision. Identity residualization removes additive effects associated with channel
identity and relative time from the targets, while topology-separated context ex-
cludes their immediate spatial and temporal neighborhood from the visible input.
We pretrain NSP on 2.2 million EEG segments from TUEG and evaluate it across
30 downstream datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, emotion recog-
nition, motor imagery, event-related potentials, cognitive-state decoding, and lan-
guage retrieval. Under full-parameter multi-task fine-tuning on EEG-FM-Bench,
NSP achieves 63.94 macro balanced accuracy across 14 datasets, exceeding the
strongest evaluated baseline by 2.35 percentage points. Controlled component
ablations assess the contribution of each mechanism, while matched context con-
trols and held-out interventions characterize the role of context geometry, signal
content, and positional information. Jointly designing latent targets and their con-

Figure 1: EEG-FM-Bench macro summary.
Electroencephalography (EEG) records millisecond-scale neu-
ral dynamics non-invasively and supports applications ranging
from clinical monitoring to emotion recognition and brain–
computer interfaces (BCIs).
Many EEG systems are still
developed for individual tasks and datasets from limited la-
beled cohorts (Lawhern et al., 2018; Song et al., 2022; 2021).
These specialized models remain useful, but often transfer
imperfectly across acquisition systems, subject populations,
and prediction targets. Inspired by self-supervised learning
in language (Brown et al., 2020; Devlin et al., 2019) and vi-
sion (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020; He et al., 2022), EEG foun-
dation models (EEG-FMs) instead pretrain reusable encoders
on broad unlabeled corpora (Kostas et al., 2021; Jiang et al.,
2024b; Wang et al., 2024; 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Yang et al.,
2023; El Ouahidi et al., 2025; Panchavati et al., 2026). EEG-
FMs have improved cross-dataset transfer, advancing general-purpose EEG representations.
Recent EEG-FMs use four main pretraining paradigms (Figure 2): (1) Contrastive learning. These
methods learn representations by bringing related EEG views closer while separating unrelated
views. BIOT (Yang et al., 2023) aligns representations across biosignal segments and modalities,
whereas BENDR (Kostas et al., 2021) contrasts masked contextual representations with their corre-
sponding latent targets. Their success nevertheless depends on how positive views, negatives, and

augmentations define invariance, and view-level agreement does not directly specify which missing
neural content should be recovered. (2) Signal reconstruction. Reconstruction objectives mask part
of an EEG recording and recover the omitted waveform, spectrum, or patch. EEGPT (Wang et al.,
2024) and REVE (El Ouahidi et al., 2025) reconstruct masked waveforms, CBraMod (Wang et al.,
2025) reconstructs EEG patches with criss-cross spatial–temporal attention, and CSBrain (Zhou
et al., 2025) reconstructs spectrogram representations. Such objectives preserve signal detail, but
may devote capacity to amplitude, noise, and other input-level variation that is not useful down-
stream. (3) Discrete or autoregressive prediction. Discrete approaches encode EEG as codebook
tokens, whereas autoregressive approaches predict the next token or patch from preceding context.
LaBraM (Jiang et al., 2024b), DeWave (Duan et al., 2023), and CodeBrain (Ma et al., 2025) learn or
use discrete EEG tokens, while ECHO (Liu et al., 2026), THD-BAR (Yang et al., 2025), and KAST-
BAR (Wang et al., 2026) predict sequential tokens or future patches. Discretization can provide
compact supervision, although its quality is bounded by the tokenizer or codebook. (4) Latent pre-
diction. These methods predict learned representations of masked regions, typically through joint-
embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) with a context and a target encoder. EEG2Rep (Moham-
madi Foumani et al., 2024) combines latent self-prediction with semantic subsequence preserving
(SSP) masking. Brain-JEPA (Dong et al., 2024) models latent brain dynamics, S-JEPA (Guetschel
et al., 2024) targets cross-dataset EEG transfer, and Laya (Panchavati et al., 2026), STST-JEPA (Se-
gal et al., 2026), and EEG-JEPA (Li et al., 2026) develop learned-target prediction for EEG with
different target construction and masking choices. PATCHCODE (Yu et al., 2026) adds discrete-
code supervision from a frozen tokenizer to continuous patch-level latent prediction. These studies
make latent prediction a promising alternative to reconstructing every detail of noisy electrophysio-
logical inputs.
Despite these advances, dependence on easily predictable signal structure can hinder the devel-
opment of EEG representations that generalize across tasks and recording conditions. Pretraining
objectives reward agreement with a chosen target, but do not by themselves distinguish transferable
neural structure from stable positional cues or local correlations. Motivated by the shared source
mixtures that volume conduction induces at neighboring scalp electrodes (Paul, 2005), we examine
local interpolation alongside prediction from channel identity, electrode coordinates, and relative
time. A masked objective may be reduced through either path without requiring broad neural con-
text. Latent prediction avoids direct waveform reconstruction, but it does not automatically remove
these low-information solutions: existing EEG JEPAs define learned targets and masked context, yet
generally do not jointly reduce additive channel- and time-conditioned components in the target and
exclude the target’s nearest spatial and temporal evidence. The central objective-design question is
therefore not only whether to predict a waveform, token, or representation, but also what information
remains in the prediction target and what evidence is available to infer it.
To address this mismatch between pretraining success and transferable representation learning, we
propose Neural State Prediction (NSP), a latent-predictive framework that jointly constrains tar-
get content and available context. An EMA-updated Target Encoder first provides stable latent
supervision for masked spatiotemporal regions. Identity residualization then removes the additive
components associated with channel identity and relative time from each target, reducing position-
conditioned predictability. In parallel, topology-separated context withholds the target’s nearest-
neighbor channels and adjacent time patches from the visible EEG content, requiring the Context
Encoder to integrate more distant evidence. The residualized target specifies what is predicted,
whereas the topology-separated context specifies from what evidence the prediction is formed. We
pretrain NSP on 2.2 million EEG segments from TUEG (Obeid & Picone, 2016) and evaluate trans-
fer across 30 downstream datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, motor imagery, emotion, cognitive

comprises 16 selected NeuralBench-EEG-Core v1.0 datasets (Banville et al., 2026) (NeuralBench
for short), after removing dataset–task pairs also covered by EEG-FM-Bench, together with the 14-
dataset EEG-FM-Bench protocol (Xiong et al., 2025). Figure 1 compares representative EEG-FMs
from all four pretraining paradigms under EEG-FM-Bench; NSP achieves 63.94 macro balanced
accuracy under full-parameter multi-task fine-tuning, outperforming the strongest evaluated base-
line by 2.35 percentage points. Matched component and context-control ablations examine how the
proposed mechanisms affect transfer, and held-out signal-content interventions and identity probes
characterize sensitivity to EEG content and the positional information retained by component vari-
ants.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We identify position-conditioned prediction and local interpolation as two low-
information paths in masked EEG latent prediction, motivating joint design of targets and
visible context.
• We propose Neural State Prediction (NSP), a latent-predictive EEG-FM pretraining
framework. Its EMA Target Encoder supplies supervision, while identity residualization
and topology-separated context jointly constrain target content and visible EEG evidence.
• We evaluate NSP across 30 downstream datasets. Under EEG-FM-Bench multi-task full
fine-tuning, it achieves 63.94 macro BAC, 2.35 percentage points above the strongest eval-
uated baseline. Matched ablations, signal-content interventions, and identity probes assess
the components and learned representations.
2
NEURAL STATE PREDICTION
Neural State Prediction (NSP) learns an EEG representation by predicting the latent states of masked
spatiotemporal regions from the remaining recording. As summarized in Figure 3, a Target Encoder
operating on the complete token grid defines the latent state to be predicted. Identity residualization
removes batch-estimated channel and relative-time components from that state, while topology-
separated context controls the evidence available to the Context Encoder. These two constructions
have complementary roles: the residualized target specifies what is predicted, and the separated
context specifies from what evidence it is inferred.
2.1
OVERVIEW AND REPRESENTATION ENCODER
Let X ∈RB×C×T be a batch of EEG segments, where B is the batch size, C is the number of
channels, and T is the number of samples per segment. Each channel is partitioned into P temporal
patches, giving the position set Ω= [P] × [C]; each position carries a d-dimensional state. For
example b, Mb ⊂Ωdenotes the target region and Gb ⊂Ωits spatial–temporal guard. Only EEG
content outside Mb ∪Gb is visible to the Context Encoder.
The Target and Context Encoders share the same architecture but have separate parameters, denoted
by ϕ and θ respectively. Their tokenizers combine three sources of information: a projection of the
EEG patch, a learned channel embedding, and adaptive channel position encoding (ACPE) from
electrode coordinates. The patch projection is the signal-dependent term. Masking replaces this
term before channel and coordinate information is added, so a masked position remains represented
in the grid without exposing its EEG content. This ordering keeps masked positions addressable by
channel and coordinate while withholding their EEG samples.
Both branches use a Cascaded Spatial–Temporal Transformer (CST). Each block applies spatial
multi-head attention (MHA) across channels, then temporal attention across patches within each
channel, followed by a feed-forward network (FFN). Temporal attention uses rotary position encod-
ing (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024). We write S = {Sb}B

EXPERIMENTS
3.1
EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Pretraining data and preprocessing. We pretrain NSP on the Temple University Hospital EEG
Corpus (TUEG), a heterogeneous clinical archive collected from 2002 to 2017 (Obeid & Picone,
2016; Wang et al., 2025).
It contains 69,652 EEG files from 14,987 subjects and 26,846 ses-
sions, recorded with variable montages and sampling rates. We map recordings to 19 standard
10–20 channels, resample to 200 Hz, apply 0.5–40 Hz band-pass and 50/60 Hz notch filtering, use
common-average referencing, clip at ±500 µV, and perform recording-level z-normalization. Non-
overlapping 6-s windows undergo quality checks after normalization. Downstream preprocessing
is benchmark specific: NeuralBench-EEG-Core follows each task’s released YAML configuration,
while EEG-FM-Bench follows its released event/channel selection, filtering, windowing, montage,
and unit-conversion pipeline; NSP uses the task-specific input adapters; the 19-channel, 200-Hz
setting specifies pretraining rather than a universal downstream input requirement.
Downstream tasks and metrics. We use NeuralBench-EEG-Core v1.0 (Banville et al., 2026) and
EEG-FM-Bench (Xiong et al., 2025) (Table 1). After removing dataset–task pairs shared with
EEG-FM-Bench, NeuralBench contributes 16 datasets: four clinical, four BCI/sensorimotor, four
event-related, and four cognitive/language tasks. Fourteen classification tasks use balanced accu-
racy (BAC); the ZuCo and Nieuwland2018 retrieval tasks use per-subject Top-5 accuracy and are
reported separately. EEG-FM-Bench contains 14 datasets from 10 paradigms and evaluates single-
task and multi-task full fine-tuning, frozen-backbone multi-task transfer, and multi-task low-rank
adaptation (LoRA).
Baselines and downstream protocols. The benchmarks use different comparison sets. Neural-
Bench evaluates BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, CBraMod, LUNA, and REVE (Kostas et al., 2021; Yang
et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025; D¨oner et al., 2025; El Ouahidi et al., 2025) with
its unified end-to-end recipe; NSP uses seeds 33–35. EEG-FM-Bench compares BENDR, BIOT,
LaBraM, EEGPT, CBraMod, CSBrain, and REVE (Kostas et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023; Jiang
et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2024; 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; El Ouahidi et al., 2025) under its four
released protocols (Xiong et al., 2025). Its 30-epoch AdamW adaptation uses a 3-epoch warmup,
batch size 128, gradient clipping at 1.0, weight decay 0.01, and a one-epoch encoder freeze. Multi-
task full fine-tuning uses seeds 42–46; other protocols use seeds 42–44. We report dataset means
with sample standard deviation (SD) and average dataset means for each macro.
Pretraining setting. The 42.83M-parameter Large model has eight CST blocks, width 512, eight
heads, FFN width 2,048, 0.2-s patches, and a predictor with hidden width 768 and output width
512. Mixed-precision distributed data-parallel training runs on eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs with
global batch size 384. AdamW uses learning rate 10−4, weight decay 0.05, gradient clipping at 1.0,
5,000 warmup steps, and cosine decay over 50,000 steps. Component studies hold data, architecture,
optimization, and transfer protocol fixed; duration and capacity studies vary only the named factor.
Appendix Tables 4–5 provide the complete configuration.

3.2
PERFORMANCE COMPARISON WITH BASELINES
To compare NSP with established EEG foundation models across domains and adaptation settings,
we evaluate it on 16 selected NeuralBench-EEG-Core datasets and the 14-dataset EEG-FM-Bench
suite. Table 2 reports the NeuralBench-EEG-Core results under its unified end-to-end protocol,
while Figure 4 summarizes single-task and multi-task full fine-tuning, plus multi-task frozen and
LoRA transfer on EEG-FM-Bench.
On the 14 NeuralBench classification tasks, NSP reaches 73.14 macro BAC, ahead of LaBraM
(70.33), CBraMod (68.04), and REVE (67.30). It has the highest mean on nine tasks and ranks
among the top two on twelve, spanning clinical, sensorimotor, event-related, and cognitive settings.
Representative wins include Mumtaz2018, Singh2021, Thielen2021, Scherer2015, Wang2017, ERP
CORE-N400, and Hinss2023. The margins range from near ties on Singh2021 and Wang2017 to
5.52 percentage points on Scherer2015 and 6.92 on Hinss2023, so the macro advantage aggregates
both modest and substantial task-level gains. NSP also reaches 12.11±0.39 and 36.27±0.12 Top-5
accuracy on ZuCo and Nieuwland2018, respectively; these retrieval scores are not pooled with BAC.
EEG-FM-Bench tests NSP under several adaptation protocols. Under full-parameter multi-task fine-
tuning, NSP averages 63.94 macro BAC, 2.35 percentage points above the strongest evaluated base-
line. Gains are largest on several clinical and BCI datasets, including TUSL, HMC, Siena, and
BCIC-2a, while emotion and motor-imagery results are more mixed; frozen and LoRA transfer are

Target construction and representation stability. To identify target-side contributions under lim-
ited labels, we evaluate frozen single-task transfer with 10% labels on TUAB, TUEV, SEED, and
PhysioMI (Table 3). Starting from block masking at 45.75 macro BAC, an EMA Target Encoder
raises the score to 51.88, and adding identity residualization further improves it to 54.24. These
cumulative changes support both stable latent supervision and removal of additive positional effects.
Removing state regularization from Full NSP lowers macro BAC from 55.70 to 46.88, indicating
that target and context design do not replace representation-stability control.
Identity residualization and context exclusion. To separate their contributions, matched rows fix
the EMA target, regularization, architecture, and visible-token budget. Residualization adds 0.62
percentage points with random exclusion and 1.52 with topology-separated exclusion. Topology
separation adds 1.06 percentage points without residualization and 1.96 with it. Both components
improve the matched means, more so together.
Signal-content and identity diagnostics. To distinguish signal sensitivity from positional informa-
tion, we zero inputs, cyclically mismatch recordings within a batch, or expand Context masks while
holding Targets fixed (Figure 17). Intervention cosine is normalized by the target-only-masked Con-
text reference. Separate probes show that channel identity remains strongly decodable from Context
states and targets without channel residualization. These component diagnostics characterize sensi-
tivity and residual identity information, not channel invariance.

CONCLUSION
NSP couples EMA-based latent prediction with identity-residualized targets and topology-separated
context to reduce additive positional effects and encourage distributed inference. Transfer across
30 datasets and component analyses support jointly designing targets and context for EEG repre-
sentation learning. Future work could adapt exclusions to signal-dependent correlations. Despite
broad benchmark coverage, responsible use requires prospective validation across populations and
acquisition settings, together with safeguards for neural-data privacy.

A
RELATED WORK
A.1
EEG FOUNDATION MODELS
EEG foundation models pretrain reusable encoders on heterogeneous, largely unlabeled recordings
and adapt them across clinical, BCI, affective, and cognitive tasks. Reconstruction-based models
differ in what they ask the encoder to preserve. EEGPT (Wang et al., 2024) and REVE (El Ouahidi
et al., 2025) recover masked waveform content, with REVE additionally encoding electrode geom-
etry to support variable layouts. CBraMod (Wang et al., 2025) reconstructs masked EEG patches
through separate spatial and temporal attention, whereas CSBrain (Zhou et al., 2025) reconstructs
spectrogram representations with specialized spatial–temporal modeling. LaBraM (Jiang et al.,
2024b) first converts EEG patches into neural tokens and predicts the masked token identities. De-
Wave (Duan et al., 2023) and CodeBrain (Ma et al., 2025) likewise introduce discrete codes that
replace direct waveform regression with code prediction. These choices determine whether supervi-
sion emphasizes sample-level detail, spectral structure, patch content, or a learned vocabulary.
Contrastive EEG foundation models specify transfer through invariance between related views
rather than reconstruction. BENDR (Kostas et al., 2021) masks the convolutional sequence and
trains a Transformer context representation to identify its corresponding latent target among within-
recording negatives. BIOT (Yang et al., 2023) tokenizes channels into a unified biosignal sequence
and aligns an original recording with a view perturbed by channel and token dropping. Contrastive
objectives can suppress nuisance variation, but the learned invariance depends on positive-pair con-
struction, negative sampling, and augmentations. This is consequential for EEG because the validity
of a transformation is task dependent, and an augmentation that is benign for one paradigm may alter
task-relevant temporal or spatial structure in another (Lashgari et al., 2020; Rommel et al., 2022).
Autoregressive EEG foundation models instead factor a recording into an ordered prediction prob-
lem. ECHO (Liu et al., 2026) uses contextual sequence-to-sequence modeling, THD-BAR (Yang
et al., 2025) organizes autoregression with topology-hierarchical structure, and KAST-BAR (Wang
et al., 2026) introduces knowledge-anchored semantic dynamics. This family can model long tempo-
ral dependencies and supports generative or next-token objectives, but its evidence path is inherently
directional. In strongly autocorrelated EEG, next-patch prediction may therefore reward accurate lo-
cal extrapolation without requiring the representation to integrate spatially distributed evidence.
A.2
LATENT PREDICTION AND JEPA
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) learn by predicting representations of unobserved
regions in a learned embedding space rather than reconstructing the input (LeCun et al., 2022).
I-JEPA established masked latent prediction for images (Assran et al., 2023), V-JEPA extended fea-
ture prediction to video (Bardes et al., 2024), and data2vec developed a related target-representation
objective across speech, vision, and language (Baevski et al., 2022). LeJEPA subsequently pro-
vided a theoretically grounded and scalable formulation with an explicit representation regular-
izer (Balestriero & LeCun, 2025; Van Assel et al., 2025).
The same predictive-state principle
now reaches world modeling: V-JEPA 2 couples large-scale latent video pretraining with an action-
conditioned predictive model for physical-world planning (Assran et al., 2025).
JEPA has also been applied to brain signals. Brain-JEPA predicts masked fMRI representations
with functional-coordinate encoding and spatiotemporal masking (Dong et al., 2024). For EEG,
S-JEPA introduces spatial block masking for cross-dataset transfer (Guetschel et al., 2024); Laya
applies latent prediction at larger scale (Panchavati et al., 2026); STST-JEPA combines shallow
EMA targets with an auxiliary reconstruction objective (Segal et al., 2026); and EEG-JEPA struc-
tures latent targets by content, support, and encoder depth (Li et al., 2026). PATCHCODE (Yu et al.,
2026) combines continuous patch-level latent prediction with auxiliary discrete-code supervision
from a frozen tokenizer; we therefore discuss it within the latent-predictive family. These methods
establish latent prediction for brain signals, but they do not combine target residualization against
channel/time identity with a context guard that excludes the target’s immediate spatial and temporal
neighborhood.

B.1
ARCHITECTURE
The NSP Large configuration has 42.83M trainable Context-side parameters, including its predictor.
The Cascaded Spatial–Temporal Transformer (CST) contains 8 blocks, each with spatial attention
(dmodel = 512, 8 heads) across channels, temporal attention with rotary position encoding (Su
et al., 2024) across patches, and a SwiGLU (Swish-gated linear unit) feed-forward sublayer with
expansion factor 4. Patch duration is 0.2 s at fs = 200 Hz. The predictor is a two-layer multilayer
perceptron (MLP) with hidden width 768, output width 512, and Gaussian error linear unit (GELU)
activation, followed by LayerNorm and ℓ2 normalization. The Target Encoder aggregates the last
three blocks (IT = {5, 6, 7}, zero-indexed). The EMA coefficient follows a cosine schedule from
0.996 to 0.9999 over the pretraining duration.

B.3
PRETRAINING HYPERPARAMETERS
Pretraining uses AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) with learning rate 1 × 10−4, weight decay
0.05, global batch size 384, gradient clipping 1.0, and 5,000 linear-warmup steps followed by cosine
annealing. Target blocks cover 50% of the token grid, with temporal spans of 2–10 patches and
spatial spans of 3–7 coordinate-near channels. The spatial guard includes the two nearest neighbors
by Euclidean distance, and the temporal guard includes adjacent patches. State regularization uses
K = 64 random unit directions with λreg = 0.1.
TUEG contains 69,652 files from 14,987 subjects and 26,846 sessions recorded with heterogeneous
clinical montages and sampling rates (Obeid & Picone, 2016). We map each usable recording
to 19 standard electrodes from the international 10–20 system and resample it to 200 Hz. After
filtering and common-average referencing, the implementation clips amplitudes to ±500 µV be-
fore recording-level z-normalization, then forms non-overlapping 6-s segments and applies quality
checks to the resulting normalized windows. Exceeding 500 µV is therefore not, by itself, a rule for
rejecting a whole segment. The pretraining collection contains 2.2M examples of shape 19 × 1,200.

the actual intervention and are used consistently throughout the paper. All configurations share the

aligned Context states and reduced effective rank. We therefore assess pretraining with downstream
transfer and representation-health measures alongside loss.

and model adapters for 14 datasets and compares single-task full fine-tuning, multi-task full fine-
tuning, frozen-backbone transfer, and LoRA. We follow each benchmark’s released task definitions
and report its results within its own protocol.

PREPROCESSING PROTOCOLS
EEG-FM-Bench (Xiong et al., 2025): Event selection, filtering, resampling, windowing, channel
mapping, and unit conversion follow the benchmark’s task/model adapter. The 19-channel, 200-
Hz specification above describes NSP pretraining, not a requirement that every downstream source

NeuralBench-EEG-Core (Banville et al., 2026): Each task uses its specified YAML configuration
for event selection, filtering, resampling, windowing, and channel mapping. Tasks are not forced to

D.2
BASELINE MODELS
We compare NSP against six official NeuralBench-EEG-Core foundation-model baselines (Table 2)
under the released benchmark protocol (Banville et al., 2026). EEG-FM-Bench uses a distinct com-
parison set that replaces LUNA with EEGPT and CSBrain (Xiong et al., 2025). All dataset-level
entries report a mean and sample standard deviation using the corresponding benchmark’s task-
specific metric definitions.
BENDR (Kostas et al., 2021) adapts wav2vec-style masked contrastive prediction to EEG. At a
masked time step, the Transformer context is trained to identify the corresponding unmasked con-
volutional representation among within-sequence negatives.
BIOT (Yang et al., 2023) tokenizes each biosignal channel into fixed-length segments and rearranges
them into a unified token sequence, allowing one encoder to process heterogeneous channel sets and
durations. Its unsupervised objective predicts an original-signal embedding from a channel- and
token-dropped view with a contrastive loss.
LaBraM (Jiang et al., 2024b) uses neural tokenization with masked prediction on large-scale het-
erogeneous EEG. A learned codebook quantizes EEG patches into discrete tokens; a Transformer
predicts masked tokens from visible context. Its pretraining corpus contains approximately 2,500
hours collected from about 20 datasets, and the model achieves strong transfer on medical tasks.
CBraMod (Wang et al., 2025) reconstructs masked EEG patches using cascaded spatial–temporal
attention. Its criss-cross Transformer applies separate spatial (cross-channel) and temporal (cross-
time) attention to the patch grid.
EEGPT (Wang et al., 2024) reconstructs masked EEG content while learning electrode-aware rep-
resentations through a target-side pretraining design. CSBrain (Zhou et al., 2025) operates on EEG
spectrograms and reconstructs masked spectral regions with specialized spatial–temporal attention.
Both models are evaluated by EEG-FM-Bench but are not part of the released NeuralBench baseline
set.
LUNA (D¨oner et al., 2025) maps variable electrode layouts into a fixed-size latent through learned
queries and cross-attention, then applies temporal attention in that topology-agnostic space. It is
pretrained on TUEG and Siena with masked-patch reconstruction.
REVE (El Ouahidi et al., 2025) combines masked waveform reconstruction with a four-dimensional
positional encoding that accommodates variable electrode locations and recording layouts. Its pre-
training corpus aggregates recordings from 92 sources and approximately 25,000 subjects.
The public-model reproduction uses the benchmark’s task-specific preprocessing and adaptation
configuration with seeds 33, 34, and 35 and checkpoint selection by the task-specific validation
metric. NSP follows the same task identities and metric definitions, with validation-selected task-
specific readouts.
D.3
ADAPTATION PROTOCOLS
Full fine-tuning: All encoder parameters and classification head are updated. This is the primary
protocol for NeuralBench-EEG-Core and EEG-FM-Bench Full FT single-task and multi-task eval-
uations.
Frozen evaluation: Encoder parameters are frozen; only classification heads are trained. EEG-FM-
Bench uses multi-task evaluation, whereas the component ablations train a head separately for each
dataset under single-task evaluation.
21

Preprint
LoRA: Low-rank adaptation (Hu et al., 2021) updates low-rank matrices injected into attention
layers while freezing the base encoder. Rank is set to 8 for all experiments.
All protocols use the corresponding validation metric for checkpoint selection and report the match-
ing test metric only on the selected checkpoint: BAC for classification and Top-5 accuracy for
retrieval.

The final study instead varies the head under full fine-tuning.

CUMULATIVE COMPONENT ABLATION

compare the cumulative configurations and the state-regularization control in Table 3. Macro BAC
rises from 44.44 for the shared-target baseline to 45.75 with block masking, 51.88 with EMA, 54.24
with identity residualization, and 55.70 for Full NSP. Task-wise changes are not uniformly positive,
and removing regularization lowers the macro to 46.88. The matched context comparisons in Table 3
separately assess exclusion geometry at a fixed visible-token budget.

MODEL SCALE AND CONTROL STUDIES
G.1
MODEL SCALE
To examine the effect of encoder capacity, we pretrain Tiny (10.74M parameters) and Medium
(24.11M) NSP models in addition to Large (42.83M), and evaluate the three scales with average
pooling under single-task full fine-tuning (Figure 15). The heatmap covers all 14 EEG-FM-Bench
datasets, and the adjacent panel averages their BAC means.
Aggregate trend favors capacity. The reported macro BAC rises from 61.76 for Tiny through 63.28
for Medium to 64.51 for Large. The increase is modest relative to the change in parameter count.
Task-level effects are heterogeneous. Figure 15 shows that Large performs best on HMC, TUAB,
Workload, PhysioMI, Things-EEG-2, ADFTD, SEED-VII, and TUSL. Medium is strongest on
TUEV, Siena, SEED-V, and Mimul-11, while Tiny leads on SEED and BCIC-2a. The aggregate
increase therefore does not imply a uniform task-wise ordering.
Scope of the scale comparison. These independently pretrained models examine capacity under
the scale-study protocol. Their full-fine-tuning results are not directly comparable with the frozen,
limited-label component ablation in Table 3. The increase in macro BAC therefore characterizes this
scale comparison, rather than quantifying a trade-off between model size and objective design.

MECHANISM DIAGNOSTICS
To complement downstream transfer results, we evaluate sensitivity to signal content and avail-
able context, and probe positional information retained by component variants. The interventions
hold Target states fixed while changing Context input. They characterize prediction sensitivity and
identity decodability, rather than demonstrate the elimination of position-only prediction or local
interpolation.
H.1
CONTEXT INTERVENTIONS AND IDENTITY PROBES
To distinguish signal sensitivity from identity decodability, we evaluate each displayed component
variant with Context interventions and linear identity probes (Figure 17). The reference Context
37

Preprint
masks target positions only; it is not an entirely unmasked input. For intervention a, relative cosine
agreement is Ra = Ca/Cref, where Ca averages prediction–target cosine over the masked target
positions and Cref is the same statistic for the reference Context. Targets are computed from the
original recordings and held fixed. Zeroing removes EEG content, while sample mismatch cyclically
shifts recordings along the batch dimension without permuting channels or time within a recording.
Spatial and temporal interventions expand the Context mask around the same targets. Negative ratios
indicate negative intervention cosine, not a negative fraction of retained information.
The probe panel reports channel and relative-time classification accuracy from full-input Context
states and constructed Target states, with chance levels 1/19 and 1/30, respectively. Context channel
accuracy remains high because residualization acts on Targets. Time-only residualization likewise
leaves channel identity largely decodable; the temporal-only baseline has neither EMA nor residu-
alization. The random-exclusion diagnostic includes residualization and corresponds to NSP with
random exclusion, not the no-residualization random control in Table 3. The shared-target baseline
and Full NSP endpoints are evaluated using the same diagnostic protocol: 512 evaluation segments
for interventions and separate sets of 256 segments for probe training and testing, with 64 sampled
tokens per segment. Sample-mismatch relative cosine changes from 0.894 to −0.028, while Tar-
get channel-probe accuracy changes from 100.00% to 14.43%. The latter remains above chance,
supporting reduced, not eliminated, identity decodability. These are single-checkpoint diagnostics
rather than estimates of variability across pretraining runs.

title: AgentRecommender: LLM Agents Enable Customizable Recommender Systems on the User Side
abstract: Recommender systems have traditionally been developed for platforms. However, this has given rise to many phenomena that may be advantageous for platform lock-in but are a nuisance to users, such as clickbait, filter bubbles, and the spread of fake news. Recently, user-side recommender systems have been proposed as a new paradigm for solving this problem. If users deploy their own recommender systems, they are no longer at the mercy of the platform's interests. However, building a user-side recommender system is not trivial; in particular, customizing one for oneself requires additional data. We propose AgentRecommender, a method that leverages the investigation capability and internal knowledge of LLM agents to flexibly build user-side recommender systems without additional data. AgentRecommender allows users to easily create recommender systems tailored to their own preferences.
content:
AgentRecommender:
LLM Agents Enable Customizable
Recommender Systems on the User Side
Ryoma Sato
rsato@nii.ac.jp
National Institute of Informatics
Abstract
Recommender systems have traditionally been developed for platforms. However, this has
given rise to many phenomena that may be advantageous for platform lock-in but are a
nuisance to users, such as clickbait, filter bubbles, and the spread of fake news. Recently,
user-side recommender systems have been proposed as a new paradigm for solving this prob-
lem. If users deploy their own recommender systems, they are no longer at the mercy of
the platform’s interests. However, building a user-side recommender system is not trivial;
in particular, customizing one for oneself requires additional data. We propose AgentRec-
ommender, a method that leverages the investigation capability and internal knowledge
of LLM agents to flexibly build user-side recommender systems without additional data.
AgentRecommender allows users to easily create recommender systems tailored to their
own preferences.
1
Introduction
Since their success at Amazon [24] and Netflix [10], recommender systems have been developed for platforms.
To increase sales, they recommend products by predicting the probability that a user will purchase them;
to keep users on the platform longer, or to make them watch more advertisements, they recommend content
by predicting expected watch time. Recommender systems have brought platforms substantial profits. It is
said that 35 percent of the sales at Amazon [30], 80 percent of the time consumed at Netflix [10], and more
than 50 percent of the content on Instagram [6] are delivered through recommender systems.
It is true that recommender systems have helped platforms grow, and users have also often been helped by
recommender systems in finding items they like. However, recommender systems have not always worked
purely in users’ favor. A recommender system that optimizes the probability of purchase may recommend
products that merely look good and do not serve the user, and in the hands of a recommender system
that maximizes expected watch time, the user may end up being shown one video after another that keeps
dragging out its conclusion. Recommender systems have also caused more serious problems, such as filter
bubbles [16, 34, 50, 52] and unfairness [12, 19, 64]. Platform operators may fix these problems immediately
when they hurt their own interests, for example when users start leaving, but otherwise they may not actively
fix them. In such cases, there is little that users can do.
To solve this problem, Sato [40] proposed user-side recommender systems, which allow users to build rec-
ommender systems with the functionality they desire by themselves.
For example, when the platform’s
recommender system delivers news biased toward a particular political party, a user-side recommender sys-
tem can balance the parties of the recommended items. When the platform’s recommender system delivers
only popular items, a user-side recommender system can recommend minor yet relevant items. Unlike the
platform, users are under severe constraints: they cannot directly access the database, nor can they obtain
the log data of other users. Sato [40] solved this problem by cleverly using the recommendation network.
However, conventional user-side recommender systems [40, 42, 44] require item labels to implement the
desired functionality. For example, when correcting for popularity, play counts or like counts can be used
directly if they are public, as on video streaming services, but a movie streaming site may not disclose view
counts. Likewise, some news sites may provide tags, but when they do not, telling which political party an
1
arXiv:2609.31166v1  [cs.IR]  25 Sep 2026

article favors is not trivial. One could resolve this by using an additional classifier, but preparing a classifier
from scratch is a heavy burden for an ordinary user.
We solve this problem by using LLM agents. Since LLM agents possess world knowledge, they can often
estimate item attributes zero-shot, and when necessary, they can estimate item attributes even more reliably
by combining this with search and other tools. By combining them with user-side recommender systems,
users can easily build recommender systems with the desired functionality. The proposed method, Agen-
tRecommender, can realize the desired functionality on the user’s side even in regimes where conventional
user-side recommender systems do not work.
2
Problem Setting
Following the setting of Sato [40], we assume that the service provider offers an item-to-item recommender
system. That is, when the page of item i ∈I is accessed, a set of related items PProv(i) ∈IK is provided,
where I is the set of all items.
The service provider’s recommender system is not necessarily fair, nor
does it necessarily have the properties the user desires. As such a system, we can exploit, for example,
Amazon’s “Customers Who Bought This Item Also Bought” section or YouTube’s "Up next" section. We
also assume that each item i has a hidden attribute ai ∈A. Any kind of attribute is conceivable: for example,
genres such as A = {“action”, “horror”, “comedy”}, eras such as A = {“1990s”, “2000s”, “2010s”, “2020s”},
popularity such as A = {“major”, “minor”}, price ranges such as A = {“low-price”, “high-price”}, and
political leanings such as A = {“Democratic”, “Republican”}. The user may design this attribute partition
arbitrarily; we make no assumptions whatsoever about the categorization and leave it to the user. This is
precisely the strength of realizing arbitrary functionality with user-side recommender systems. We assume
that the user wants the recommended items to have these attributes in specific proportions, to be balanced, or
to achieve higher coverage in the sense that at least one item from each category is recommended. The service
provider’s recommender system does not necessarily respect these constraints. Under such circumstances,
the user builds a recommender system that respects the desired constraints. A user who is tired of being
recommended only famous items may specify popularity as the category so as to receive recommendations
with balanced popularity, and a user who is fed up with recommendations biased toward a particular political
leaning may specify political leaning as the category so as to receive politically balanced recommendations.
The major difference from previous user-side recommender systems is that we assume the attribute ai ∈A
is not observable to the user, in contrast to what previous user-side recommender systems assumed. This
drastically reduces the amount of data the user needs to build a recommender system. The attributes ai ∈A
are observed only at evaluation time, where we evaluate how well the recommender system built by the user
satisfies the constraints.
In summary, the problem setting is stated as follows.
Given: Oracle access to the official recommendations Pprov; the attribute space A and the constraints
to be satisfied, specified by the user in natural language; and a budget B. The attribute ai ∈A of
each item is not observed at construction time and is referred to only at evaluation time.
Output: A user-side recommender system Q: I →IK that satisfies the constraints on A.
Internally, Q may evaluate Pprov at most B times per recommendation.
For simplicity, we consider user-side item-to-item recommendation here, but user-side user-to-item recom-
mendation can be constructed in the same manner.
3
Proposed Method: AgentRecommender
The proposed method, AgentRecommender, uses an LLM agent to build a recommendation list that satisfies
the constraints on the item attributes A while using the service provider’s recommender system Pprov (Figure
1). AgentRecommender repeatedly observes Pprov(j) of an item j that the LLM deems promising and adds
it to the candidates, thereby gradually collecting promising items, and in the end, the LLM constructs a list
that satisfies the conditions from the candidates. This process can also be viewed as an LLM agent actively

exploring the recommendation network, i.e., the graph whose nodes are the items and in which an edge is
drawn from i to j when item j is recommended on the page of item i.
Suppose the user accesses the page of item i. The service provider’s recommendations L = Pprov(i) ∈IK
can then be observed from the DOM, HTTP requests, and the like. Starting from this list as the initial list,
we repeat the following operations B times using the LLM:
1. Present to the LLM, in natural language, the items in the current list that have not yet been
expanded together with the requirements, and let it select the item to expand.
2. Access the page of the selected item j behind the browser, obtain the service provider’s recommen-
dations Pprov(j) ∈IK, and add them to the list L.
Finally, we present the items of L obtained so far and the requirements to the LLM, and let it select the K
items that should ultimately be presented to the user.
Only the item names are given to the LLM, but the LLM estimates the attributes of the items using its
internal knowledge (and, if necessary, tool calls such as search) and selects the item that should be explored

formance than the service provider’s recommender system and than merely re-ranking it, across the three
domains of MovieLens 1M (movies), LastFM (music), and Amazon Home and Kitchens (e-commerce) and
the three criteria of oldness, genre, and price. This shows that even when the service provider’s recommender
system does not offer a particular functionality, users can build a recommender system with the desired func-
tionality on their own.
